analysis.one_liner: Writes skimpy short-term health insurance plans into federal law, exempt from most consumer protections.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on October 23, 2019 and never moved again before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1] [S5].
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put into permanent law a 2018 rule that lets insurers sell short-term, limited-duration health plans for up to 12 months at a time, renewable for up to three years total [S2] [S3]. These plans are exempt from the rules that govern regular insurance under the Affordable Care Act: they can refuse people with pre-existing conditions, skip required benefits, and cap payouts [S2]. The bill would also stop any future administration from reversing the rule by regulation, because the expanded definition would be written directly into statute [S3]. It never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in committee until the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Insurers that sell short-term plans, and brokers who market them, gain a permanent legal foundation for a product line with lighter regulation and lower compliance costs than ACA-compliant plans. Some younger, healthier people who do not expect to need much care would be able to buy cheaper coverage than ACA plans.

how_it_helps.text: The bill writes the definition of short-term limited-duration insurance directly into the Public Health Service Act, allowing plans of less than 12 months that can be renewed for up to 3 years total [S3].
This codifies the 2018 rule from Treasury, Labor, and HHS that raised the maximum duration of such plans from under 3 months to up to 12 months with renewals up to 36 months [S2].
Writing the rule into statute means it could no longer be reversed by a future administration through the regulatory process [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People with pre-existing conditions or serious health needs: short-term plans are exempt from ACA rules requiring coverage of pre-existing conditions and essential benefits, and they can deny claims or cap what they pay. ACA-compliant policyholders also bear costs indirectly, because when healthier people move to cheaper short-term plans, the ACA risk pool shrinks and premiums for everyone left in it rise.

drawbacks.text: Short-term plans are exempt from the ACA's consumer protections, so they can exclude pre-existing conditions, omit required benefits like prescription drugs or maternity care, and cap annual payouts — gaps buyers often discover only when they get sick [S2].

The plans are designed as a cheaper alternative to ACA-compliant coverage, which pulls healthier people out of the ACA risk pool and raises premiums for the people who remain, particularly those who are older or have health problems [S2].
A buyer can be left mid-treatment when a short-term plan expires or is not renewed, since the coverage is temporary by definition [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers cheaper premiums to a narrow group of healthy buyers and a durable market to the insurers that serve them. The costs fall on a broader and sicker group: people who are denied coverage or shortchanged by short-term plans, and everyone in the ACA market whose premiums rise as the pool thins out. Making the arrangement permanent in statute, rather than leaving it as a reversible regulation, outweighs the narrow benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Health Subcommittee, and sat there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Representative Andy Biggs (R-AZ) introduced the bill on October 23, 2019 [S1] [S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and three days later to that committee's Subcommittee on Health [S5].
Two Republican members cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who depend on ACA protections — coverage of pre-existing conditions, required benefits, and a stable risk pool — are better off that the bill never advanced, since it would have locked in lighter-regulated plans and made the ACA rule changes irreversible by future administrations. Insurers selling short-term plans did not get the statutory entrenchment they sought, though the underlying 2018 rule remained in effect.

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to write the expanded short-term plan definition into statute

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it remained in committee until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: Only Republicans backed the bill — one sponsor and two cosponsors, all R — and it died in a committee controlled by Democrats without any vote.

industries.note: The bill would give their product a permanent statutory foundation, up to 12 months of coverage renewable to 3 years, with none of the ACA's rules on pre-existing conditions, benefits, or payout limits. Their gain comes from selling cheaper, skimpier coverage, the cost of which falls on people who get sick and on ACA enrollees left in a thinner risk pool.

Short-term plans compete with ACA-compliant coverage for healthier customers; the bill would lock in that competition on unequal terms, pushing premiums up in the ACA-compliant market as healthier people leave.
A permanent, statutorily defined short-term plan market expands the products brokers can sell, including to consumers who may not understand the coverage gaps.
